 Tesla Rebrands "Full Self-Driving" to "Tesla Assisted Driving" Across Europe
 A Name Change to Meet Regulatory Concerns Why "Full Self-Driving" Drew Criticism A Campaign for Approval Patchwork Access Across Nations EU-Wide Vote Delayed Until December U.S. Keeps the Original Name What the Shift Means for the Future
 By Mark Lim Published 3 days ago • 3 min read Photo by Prometheus 🔥 on Unsplash Tesla has formally dropped the controversial "Full Self-Driving" label across its European websites, rebranding the feature as "Tesla Assisted Driving" to address concerns from regulators that the old name was misleading. The change, confirmed following disclosures from German authorities, marks a significant concession to transparency and a calculated step toward securing approval for the system across the entire European Union. Pages for Germany, Spain, the Netherlands, and Slovakia now redirect to the new designation, while the United States market continues to use "Full Self-Driving (Supervised)."
 Why the Name Became a Problem
 For years, critics have argued that "Full Self-Driving" promises capabilities the system does not yet possess. Despite the bold title, the technology requires constant human supervision ; drivers remain fully legally responsible for vehicle operation at all times. Regulators across multiple countries have warned that the branding could reasonably lead buyers to believe the car is capable of SAE Level 3 or higher autonomy, where the system can take full control under defined conditions, when it operates only at Level 2.
 Italy : Authorities noted internally that the name, combined with promotional materials, "could lead users to believe that the vehicle is equipped with unsupervised automatic driving functions."
 Sweden : Consumer protection authorities asked the Transport Agency to assess whether marketing was creating false impressions of autonomy.
 Norway : A Tesla owner wrote to the Public Roads Administration seeking clarity, urging: "Please do not simply say again that 'we are waiting for the EU' without explaining what Tesla or Norway must deliver in the meantime."
 A Campaign to Win Approval
 The rebrand is part of a broader, coordinated effort to bring the system to European roads. As Reuters reported this week, Tesla has encouraged owners and supporters to lobby national regulators for faster approvals, building a groundswell of public support alongside technical submissions. CEO Elon Musk has repeatedly described the technology as central to Tesla’s long‑term value and growth, making European rollout a top strategic priority. Germany confirmed on Tuesday that Tesla had offered the name change as part of its engagement with authorities, signalling a willingness to adjust its presentation to meet standards.
 Approval Status: Eight Nations In, More to Follow
 The system is already authorised in eight EU countries , with Slovakia poised to become the ninth within days. However, harmonised approval across all 27 member states has proven more complex than anticipated. A scheduled vote on EU‑wide deployment has been pushed back from October to at least December , with countries including France conducting additional testing to verify safety and compliance. The delay underscores differing approaches across the bloc some nations moving quickly and others insisting on deeper scrutiny.
 Two Names, One System
 Notably, the rebrand is Europe‑only for now. Tesla’s U.S. website continues to list the feature as "Full Self‑Driving (Supervised)," retaining the original moniker with a parenthetical qualifier. This split highlights the challenge of marketing advanced driver assistance across jurisdictions with different regulatory cultures and consumer protection frameworks. The system itself has not changed only what it is called. The shift acknowledges that words matter: what reads as aspirational in one market can read as deceptive in another.
 The new name "Tesla Assisted Driving" aligns more closely with how independent experts describe the technology: a powerful suite of aids that enhances safety and convenience, but does not replace the driver. Whether the change will satisfy every regulator remains to be seen; France’s ongoing testing suggests technical questions persist beyond branding. Yet the rebrand sends a clear signal: Tesla is adapting its language to meet European standards, not the other way around. As the December vote approaches, the world will be watching to see whether a more modest name opens the door to a continent‑wide rollout.
